clinicalPearls: A prenatally lethal form of multiple pterygium syndrome with severe foetal akinesia, multiple contractures and extensive webbing across joints
Foetal hydrops, cystic hygroma and generalised oedema are characteristic and often lead to intrauterine or early neonatal death
Pulmonary hypoplasia from absent foetal breathing movements is a usual cause of death
Craniofacial features include hypertelorism, micrognathia, a small mouth and low-set ears
Most commonly caused by autosomal recessive variants in acetylcholine receptor subunit genes, particularly CHRNG, with CHRNA1 and CHRND also implicated
It lies at the severe end of the spectrum whose milder counterpart is Escobar (non-lethal) syndrome
Management is supportive and palliative, with the emphasis on accurate diagnosis, postmortem confirmation and genetic counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Lethal multiple pterygium syndrome is caused by severe loss of function in genes encoding subunits of the foetal acetylcholine receptor, most often CHRNG (gamma subunit) but also CHRNA1 and CHRND. Complete failure of foetal neuromuscular transmission abolishes foetal movement during a critical developmental period. The profound akinesia produces multiple joint contractures, webbing across the flexed joints, pulmonary hypoplasia from absent breathing movements, and impaired lymphatic drainage manifesting as cystic hygroma, hydrops and generalised oedema. The completeness of the receptor defect explains why this form is lethal in utero or shortly after birth, in contrast to the survivable Escobar variant.
additionalDifferentials: Pena-Shokeir syndrome / foetal akinesia deformation sequence
Congenital myasthenic syndromes with severe prenatal onset
additionalInvestigations: Detailed prenatal ultrasound showing akinesia, contractures, webbing, hydrops and cystic hygroma
Postmortem/foetal examination with clinical photographs to confirm the phenotype
Molecular genetic testing for CHRNG, CHRNA1 and CHRND and a foetal akinesia panel
Chromosomal microarray or karyotype to exclude aneuploidy
Muscle and nerve histology if the neuromuscular basis is uncertain
Placental and lymphatic assessment where hydrops is present
redFlags: Foetal hydrops and cystic hygroma indicating a lethal course
Severe pulmonary hypoplasia incompatible with postnatal survival
Recurrence in subsequent pregnancies given autosomal recessive inheritance
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is uniformly poor, with death occurring in utero or in the early neonatal period; care is supportive and palliative, and the priority is establishing a genetic diagnosis to inform recurrence risk and prenatal options.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish the lethal form from the survivable Escobar variant when counselling
Not securing genetic confirmation, leaving recurrence risk uncertain
Overlooking the autosomal recessive one-in-four recurrence risk
Missing the opportunity for postmortem examination to guide future pregnancies
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
Gorlin's Syndromes of the Head and Neck
management: Comfort-focused palliative care given the uniformly lethal prognosis in utero or the early neonatal period
Confirmation of the genetic diagnosis by testing of CHRNG, CHRNA1 and CHRND and a foetal akinesia panel to guide counselling
Perinatal palliative care planning and bereavement support for the family
Non-directive genetic counselling regarding the autosomal recessive recurrence risk
Offer of prenatal diagnosis and preimplantation genetic testing in future pregnancies
Multidisciplinary involvement of foetal medicine, neonatology, clinical genetics and palliative care
